analogy.p: Ionic bonding is like one person giving a toy to another: afterwards one has a surplus (positive) and one has a deficit (negative), and the attraction between them holds the pair together. Covalent bonding is like two people sharing a pair of headphones: each gets what they need because they share it. Metallic bonding is like a crowd of fixed stalls (ions) with customers (electrons) wandering freely between them while still being drawn to the stalls. Where it breaks down: real electrons are not objects handed over, and in real ionic compounds the ions attract each other in all directions, not just in pairs.

bullets: **Ionic bonding**: a **metal** reacts with a **non-metal**. The particles are **oppositely charged ions**, formed by **electron transfer**.
**Covalent bonding**: between **non-metal atoms**. The particles are **atoms which share pairs of electrons**.
**Metallic bonding**: in **metals** and **alloys**. The particles are **positive metal ions surrounded by a sea of delocalised electrons**.
All three involve **strong forces**: this is why bonds are hard to break, and why they should never be confused with the weak **intermolecular forces** between simple molecules.
A quick decision rule: metal + non-metal = ionic; non-metal + non-metal = covalent; metal only = metallic.

Each type produces a different kind of structure: **giant ionic lattices**, **simple molecules, giant covalent structures or polymers**, and **giant metallic lattices**. These structures explain properties like melting point and conductivity in the next spec points.
Bonding is about **outer shell electrons**, so you need to be able to write electronic structures such as sodium 2,8,1 or chlorine 2,8,7.
core.h: The three types of strong chemical bond
core.p: Atoms join together because their outer electrons can be rearranged to give a more stable arrangement, usually a **full outer shell** like a noble gas. There are three types of **strong chemical bond** you must know: **ionic**, **covalent** and **metallic**. Which one forms depends on whether the atoms involved are metals or non-metals, and what the electrons do: they are **transferred**, **shared in pairs** or **delocalised** (free to move through the whole structure).

bullets: Sodium (atomic number 11) is **2,8,1**: it has **1 outer electron**, so it is easier to **lose 1** than to gain 7.
Chlorine (17) is **2,8,7**: it has **7 outer electrons**, so it is easier to **gain 1** than to lose 7.
Magnesium (12) is **2,8,2** and oxygen (8) is **2,6**: magnesium loses 2 and oxygen gains 2.
The **group number** equals the number of outer electrons, so metals in **Group 1 lose 1**, **Group 2 lose 2**, and non-metals in **Group 7 gain 1**, **Group 6 gain 2**.
An atom becomes an **ion** when it gains or loses electrons: the number of protons does not change, so the **charge** is the difference between protons and electrons.
After ion formation the particle has the electronic structure of the **nearest noble gas**: Na+ (2,8) is like neon, Cl- (2,8,8) is like argon.
**Non-metals in Group 4 and 5** (and hydrogen) mostly **share** electrons because they would need to gain or lose too many.
core.h: Why atoms bond: full outer shells and electronic structures
core.p: Noble gases in Group 0 are unreactive because their outer shells are full (2 electrons for helium, 8 for the others). Other atoms react to reach this stable arrangement by **losing**, **gaining** or **sharing** electrons. To predict what happens you work out the **electronic structure** from the atomic number, filling shells in order: 2 in the first shell, 8 in the second, 8 in the third (to calcium).

bullets: **Na (2,8,1) loses 1 electron to form Na+ (2,8)**; **Cl (2,8,7) gains 1 electron to form Cl- (2,8,8)**.
The ionic bond is the **electrostatic attraction between Na+ and Cl-**, not the transferred electron itself.
Ions formed from **Group 1 have a charge of 1+**, **Group 2 have 2+**, **Group 6 have 2-** and **Group 7 have 1-**.
**Metals form positive ions** because they lose electrons; **non-metals form negative ions** because they gain electrons.
The reaction is a **redox process**: the metal is oxidised (loses electrons) and the non-metal is reduced (gains electrons). This idea returns in the reactivity and electrolysis topics.
Ionic compounds are **neutral overall**: the total positive charge equals the total negative charge.
core.p: When a metal reacts with a non-metal, the **metal atoms lose electrons** to become **positively charged ions (cations)** and the **non-metal atoms gain those electrons** to become **negatively charged ions (anions)**. The two types of ion are held together by the **strong electrostatic force of attraction between oppositely charged ions**. This force is what the ionic bond actually is. Sodium chloride is the standard example.

bullets: **Sodium chloride**: Na loses its one outer electron; Cl gains it. Draw **[Na]+** with its 8 outer electrons (crosses) and **[Cl]-** with 8 (7 dots and 1 cross).
**Magnesium oxide, MgO**: Mg transfers **2 electrons** to O. Draw **[Mg]2+** and **[O]2-**, each with 8 outer electrons.
**Magnesium chloride, MgCl2**: Mg transfers **1 electron to each of two Cl atoms**, so there are **one Mg2+ and two Cl-**.
**Sodium oxide, Na2O**: **two Na atoms** each transfer 1 electron to **one O atom**: Na+, Na+, and O2-.
Always show **square brackets** and the **charge** on every ion; do not draw a bond line between ions.
Show only the **outer shell** electrons, unless the question asks for full electronic structures.
Check: the **numbers of electrons lost equal the number gained**.
core.h: Dot and cross diagrams for ionic compounds
core.p: A **dot and cross diagram** shows the **outer electrons** of the atoms and where they end up. One type of electron (for example from the metal) is drawn as crosses and the other (from the non-metal) as dots, so you can see the transfer. For the ion, you draw the **full outer shell in square brackets with the charge at the top right**. In the exam you are expected to draw these for compounds of **Group 1 and 2 metals with Group 6 and 7 non-metals**.

bullets: **Sodium chloride** has Na+ and Cl- in a **1:1** ratio, so the formula is **NaCl**.
**Magnesium chloride**: Mg2+ needs **two** Cl-, so **MgCl2**.
**Sodium oxide**: O2- needs **two** Na+, so **Na2O**.
**Aluminium oxide**: Al3+ and O2- need a ratio of **2 Al3+ : 3 O2-** (6+ and 6-), giving **Al2O3**.
**Method**: write the ions with charges, find the lowest common multiple of the charges, then work out how many of each ion are needed.
A **diagram of a lattice** shows a small part of the structure; the pattern continues in all directions.
You may be given a **diagram or model** and asked to work out the formula by counting the ions or using the ratio.
Ionic compounds are **solids at room temperature** because a lot of energy is needed to overcome the strong attractions.
core.h: Ionic compounds: giant lattices and formulae
core.p: An ionic compound is not made of separate molecules. It is a **giant ionic lattice**: a huge **regular arrangement of positive and negative ions**, with each ion attracted to its oppositely charged neighbours in **all directions** by strong electrostatic forces. The formula of the compound shows the **simplest ratio** of ions (the **empirical formula**), and it is found by balancing the charges so that the compound is neutral.

bullets: **Hydrogen, H2**: two H atoms share **one pair**: H-H. Each H gets 2 electrons, a full first shell.
**Chlorine, Cl2**: one shared pair; each Cl has **three non-bonding (lone) pairs**.
**Oxygen, O2**: a **double bond** (two shared pairs): O=O.
**Nitrogen, N2**: a **triple bond**: N with three shared pairs, and one lone pair on each N.
**Hydrogen chloride, HCl**: one shared pair between H and Cl.

**Water, H2O**: O shares one pair with each H; O has **two lone pairs**. **Ammonia, NH3**: N shares one pair with each of three H; N has **one lone pair**. **Methane, CH4**: C shares one pair with each of four H.
**Carbon dioxide, CO2**: **each O is double bonded to C**: O=C=O.
The number of bonds an atom usually forms equals the number of electrons it needs for a full outer shell: **H 1, O 2, N 3, C 4, Cl 1**.
core.h: Covalent bonding: sharing pairs of electrons
core.p: Non-metal atoms bond covalently by **sharing pairs of electrons**, so that each atom has a **full outer shell**. A **covalent bond** is the **strong electrostatic attraction between the shared pair of electrons and the nuclei of the bonded atoms**. A single bond is one shared pair, a **double bond** is two shared pairs and a triple bond is three. Covalent substances may be **small molecules, polymers or giant covalent structures**.

bullets: Draw the **outer shell** of each atom as a circle, overlapping where bonds form.
Put **two electrons (one dot and one cross) in each overlap** for a single bond; four electrons for a double bond; six for a triple bond.
Show **lone pairs** (non-bonding pairs) on the atoms: for example, **four electrons (two pairs) on the O in water**.
Check that **every atom has a full outer shell**: hydrogen has 2, the others 8.
Count the electrons: **water** has 8 around oxygen (2 shared pairs plus 2 lone pairs).
Do not draw **ions** or brackets for covalent molecules; the particles are neutral.
Be careful with **O2 and N2**: show two overlapping pairs (O2) or three (N2) between the atoms.
core.h: Dot and cross diagrams for covalent molecules
core.p: In a covalent dot and cross diagram, the outer shells of the atoms **overlap** and the shared electrons sit in the overlap region. Electrons from one atom are drawn as dots and from the other as crosses so you can see where each shared electron comes from. You must be able to draw **hydrogen, chlorine, oxygen, nitrogen, hydrogen chloride, water, ammonia and methane**.

bullets: **Displayed formula** (e.g. H-O-H): shows **which atoms are bonded** and the **number of bonds**; it does not show the **3D shape**, the **size of atoms** or the **electrons**.

**Ball and stick model**: shows the **3D arrangement** and **bond angles**; it does not show the **electrons**, and the sticks suggest bonds are physical objects with gaps between atoms, which is not true.

**Dot and cross diagram**: shows **which electrons are shared** and which atom they come from; it does not show the **shape** or **relative size**, and dots and crosses are identical electrons really.
**Space-filling models** (if shown) are more realistic about size but hide the bonds.
Giant covalent structures such as **diamond** and **silicon dioxide** are drawn with sticks as a repeating network in three dimensions.
To find the molecular formula from a model, **count each type of atom**: a model with 1 C and 4 H gives **CH4**.
When asked for the **limitations**, name the model and give a specific feature it cannot show.
core.h: Representing covalent bonds: sticks, 2D and 3D models
core.p: Chemists use several models to show covalent bonds. **Displayed formulae** show atoms as symbols and each covalent bond as a **line (stick)**. **Ball and stick models** show atoms as balls and bonds as sticks, in **three dimensions**. **Dot and cross diagrams** show the electrons. Each model has **strengths and limitations**, and you are expected to comment on them. You should also be able to deduce the **molecular formula** of a substance from a diagram or model.

bullets: Metal atoms **lose their outer electrons** to join the shared pool, becoming positive ions (e.g. Na+, Mg2+).
The delocalised electrons come from the outer shell, so **magnesium contributes 2 per atom**, sodium 1 per atom.
The **strong attraction** between ions and electrons explains the **high melting and boiling points** of most metals.
The electrons are free to move, so metals **conduct electricity** and also **conduct heat** well.
The layers of ions can **slide over each other** while staying bonded, so metals are **malleable and ductile**.
**Alloys** are mixtures of metals with different-sized atoms that distort the layers, making them **harder**.
Metallic bonding is found only in **metals and alloys**; do not describe it as electron transfer or sharing between two atoms.
core.p: Metals have a **giant structure** in which the atoms are arranged in **regular layers**. The outer electrons of each atom are **delocalised**: they are not attached to a particular atom and are free to move through the structure. The metal is therefore made of **positive metal ions in a lattice surrounded by a sea of delocalised electrons**. **Metallic bonding** is the **strong electrostatic attraction between the positive metal ions and the delocalised electrons**.

bullets: **Ionic**: metal + non-metal; **ions**; electrons **transferred**; **giant ionic lattice**; **strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions**.
**Covalent**: non-metal + non-metal; **atoms**; electrons **shared in pairs**; **simple molecules or giant covalent**; **strong covalent bonds** within the molecule.
**Metallic**: metals; **positive ions and delocalised electrons**; **giant metallic lattice**.
**Simple molecular substances** have strong bonds **within** molecules but only weak **intermolecular forces** between them, so they have **low melting and boiling points**.
**Ionic and giant covalent** substances have strong forces throughout, so very high melting points.
**Electrical conductivity** depends on **charged particles that are free to move**: ionic compounds only conduct when molten or dissolved, metals conduct as solids.
The **state of a substance** (solid, liquid, gas) at room temperature gives clues about its bonding.
core.p: A very common exam task is to **compare and contrast** the types of bonding or to decide which bonding a substance has from information about its properties or elements. Use the **types of element, the particles and what happens to the electrons**, and then link to the structure. Remember to talk about **forces between particles** rather than 'bonds break' when talking about simple molecules.

bullets: **Formulae in equations**: you need the formulae of ionic compounds to write balanced equations (for example 2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO).
**Half equations** show the transfer of electrons: Na -> Na+ + e-; Cl2 + 2e- -> 2Cl-.
**Electrolysis**: ionic compounds conduct only when **molten or in solution** because the ions are free to move.
**Periodic table**: elements in the same group form ions with the same charge because they have the same number of outer electrons.
**Organic chemistry**: carbon forms **four covalent bonds**, giving molecules such as methane and polymers.
**Nanoscience and materials**: the type of bonding explains why materials (diamond, graphite, metals, ceramics) are used for particular jobs.
**Common confusion**: **ionic bonds are not 'electrons shared' and covalent bonds are not 'electrons transferred'**.
core.h: Links to other topics and Higher tier thinking
core.p: Bonding underpins much of the chemistry course. It links to the periodic table (the group number tells you the ion charge), to chemical equations (formulae of ionic compounds), to electrolysis (ions must be free to move), to the reactivity series (metals lose electrons) and to organic chemistry (covalent bonding in hydrocarbons). Higher-tier questions often ask for **extended explanations** that join structure, bonding and properties.

exam: **1-mark**: name the type of bonding (ionic, covalent or metallic) from the elements involved. Use the metal/non-metal rule.
**2-mark 'describe how ions are formed'**: state that the atom **loses (or gains) electrons**, and give the **charge** or the **full outer shell** it ends with.

**Dot and cross diagrams (2 to 3 marks)**: correct number of **outer electrons**, **square brackets with charges** for ions, **overlap with shared pairs** for covalent molecules, and **correct number of ions** (e.g. two Cl- with Mg2+).
**Formula questions**: show the ion charges and balance them: 'Mg2+ and Cl- so MgCl2'. A mark is often given for the working.
**4-mark 'describe the bonding in sodium chloride'**: electron transfer from Na to Cl; forms Na+ and Cl-; **strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions**; giant lattice.
**Covalent description**: 'a pair of electrons is shared between two non-metal atoms; this is a strong covalent bond; each atom gets a full outer shell'.
**Metallic description**: 'positive ions in a regular lattice, surrounded by a sea of delocalised electrons, with strong electrostatic attraction between them'.
**Limitations of models (2 to 3 marks)**: name the model and a **specific** thing it cannot show, for example 'ball and stick does not show the electrons or the relative size of atoms'.
**Command words**: **describe** (what), **explain** (why, using attraction between particles), **compare** (similarities and differences using linking words like 'whereas').
Use the **key words** 'electrostatic', 'oppositely charged ions', 'shared pair' and 'delocalised electrons' because mark schemes look for them.
Do not write 'bonds' when you mean 'intermolecular forces' for simple molecules.

mistakes.r: Ionic bonding is the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions formed by electron transfer.
mistakes.w: Ionic bonding is the sharing of electrons.

mistakes.r: The bond is the force of attraction between the oppositely charged ions, not the electron.
mistakes.w: An ionic bond is the electron that is transferred.

mistakes.r: Covalent bonds are strong; it is the weak intermolecular forces between molecules that are overcome when they melt.
mistakes.w: Covalent bonds are weak, which is why molecular substances melt easily.

mistakes.r: Metals lose electrons and form positive ions; non-metals gain electrons and form negative ions.
mistakes.w: Metals lose electrons so they become negative.

mistakes.r: Sodium chloride is a giant ionic lattice of Na+ and Cl- ions; draw ions in brackets with charges and no bond line.
mistakes.w: Draw sodium chloride as a molecule NaCl with a line between Na and Cl.

mistakes.r: Metallic bonding is the attraction between positive metal ions and a sea of delocalised electrons.
mistakes.w: Metallic bonding is electrons moving between two atoms.

mistakes.r: Write each ion in square brackets with the charge at the top right, showing full outer shells.
mistakes.w: Forgetting the charge or the brackets on the ions in a dot and cross diagram.

mistakes.r: Mg2+ needs two Cl-, so the formula is MgCl2.
mistakes.w: The formula of magnesium chloride is MgCl.

mistakes.r: Atoms are not alive and do not want things; say they gain, lose or share electrons to achieve a full outer shell, which is more stable.
mistakes.w: Atoms want a full shell, so they feel like gaining electrons.

summary: You must describe ionic bonding (electron transfer and electrostatic attraction between ions), covalent bonding (shared pairs of electrons between non-metal atoms) and metallic bonding (positive ions and delocalised electrons), draw dot and cross diagrams, work out formulae and evaluate bonding models. It matters because bonding explains the structure and properties of every substance in the course.

terms.d: The strong electrostatic force of attraction between oppositely charged ions.
A strong bond between non-metal atoms formed by a shared pair of electrons.
The strong electrostatic attraction between positive metal ions and delocalised electrons.
An atom or group of atoms that has gained or lost electrons and so has an overall charge.
A positively charged ion, formed when an atom loses electrons.
A negatively charged ion, formed when an atom gains electrons.
Electrons that are not attached to one atom and are free to move through a structure.
A huge regular three-dimensional arrangement of oppositely charged ions held by strong electrostatic forces.
The force of attraction between opposite charges.
A diagram showing the outer electrons of atoms, using dots and crosses to show where they come from.
A pair of outer-shell electrons that are not involved in bonding.
A covalent bond in which two pairs of electrons are shared.
A small group of atoms joined by covalent bonds, such as H2O or CO2.
A large network of atoms joined by covalent bonds, such as diamond.
The simplest whole-number ratio of atoms or ions in a compound.
The arrangement of electrons in shells around an atom, such as 2,8,1.
An unreactive Group 0 element with a full outer shell of electrons.
A weak force of attraction between molecules, much weaker than a covalent bond.
A mixture of a metal with another element, usually another metal.

worked.ans: Magnesium transfers one electron to each of two chlorine atoms, forming Mg2+ and two Cl- ions, each with a full outer shell (8 electrons). The ions are held together by strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions. Formula: MgCl2.
worked.q: Describe, with a dot and cross diagram, how magnesium and chlorine bond to form magnesium chloride. (4 marks)
steps: Magnesium is 2,8,2 (2 outer electrons) and chlorine is 2,8,7 (7 outer electrons).
Mg loses 2 electrons to form Mg2+ (2,8).
Each Cl gains 1 electron to form Cl- (2,8,8); two Cl atoms are needed for the 2 electrons.
Diagram: [Mg]2+ with 8 crosses, between two [Cl]- each with 7 dots and 1 cross.
Ionic bond: the strong electrostatic attraction between Mg2+ and the Cl- ions.

worked.q: Work out the formulae of (a) aluminium oxide, containing Al3+ and O2-, and (b) potassium oxide, containing K+ and O2-. (2 marks)
steps: (a) Find the lowest common multiple of 3 and 2: 6.
Check: 2 x (3+) = 6+ and 3 x (2-) = 6-, so the charges cancel.
(b) O2- needs two K+ to balance: 2 x (1+) = 2+.

worked.ans: Ball and stick models show the three-dimensional arrangement and the three N-H bonds, so the formula NH3 can be found. However, they do not show the electrons, such as the shared pairs or the lone pair on nitrogen, and the sticks imply physical connections that do not exist. A dot and cross diagram is better for showing the electrons.
worked.q: A student says ball and stick models are the best way to show a molecule of ammonia, NH3. Evaluate this statement. (3 marks)
steps: Ball and stick shows the 3D shape: the N in the middle with three H atoms around it.
It shows the number of bonds (three) so the molecular formula can be deduced.
But it does not show the electrons, so you cannot see the lone pair on N or which atom each shared electron came from.
The sticks also wrongly suggest there are physical rods and a gap between atoms.
